title: The Reunion
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of erased memory and unnoticed absence
excerpt: The reunion was a small mistake. Marcus had gone because his wife told him to. He had, on arriving, been immediately identified by three former classmates, and had been embraced. He was, by eight-fifteen, at the small bar with a glass of wine, when Anna asked if he had seen Jonas yet. He had said: Jonas? Anna had said: Marcus. Jonas Weber. Your Jonas.

chapters.title: Someone I Should Remember
chapters.body:
The reunion was a small mistake.

Marcus Hoffmann was thirty-eight, and he had, at eighteen, graduated from a small gymnasium in a small town outside Freiburg, and had, in the twenty years since, become the sort of adult his eighteen-year-old self would not have expected — a small careful municipal architect in Hamburg with a small careful marriage and two small careful children. He had, over those twenty years, kept in touch with almost none of his classmates. He had, on receiving the invitation to the twenty-year reunion in March, spent perhaps three minutes considering whether to reply. He had, in his small careful way, replied yes because his wife had said he ought to, and because a small part of him — a part he did not entirely trust — had wanted to see who had become who.

The reunion had been on a Saturday in June, at the small restaurant near the gymnasium that had, for reasons of small tradition, hosted such reunions since the nineteen-eighties. Marcus had driven down that afternoon. He had, on arriving, gone to the small hotel where the classmates had reserved a small block of rooms. He had, at seven, walked to the restaurant.

He had, on entering, been immediately identified by three former classmates — Anna, Klaus, and Sabine — and had, in the specific small polite way of a man being welcomed back into a small forgotten social world, been embraced.

He had, over the following hour, been reintroduced to perhaps thirty of his forty-two former classmates. He had been surprised to find that he remembered most of them. He had been more surprised to find that most of them remembered him. He had, in the small careful way of a man who had not thought about his gymnasium years in a long time, been pleased by this.

He had, at eight-fifteen, been standing near the small bar with a small glass of white wine, when Anna had come up to him and had said, in her small pleasant voice: *have you seen Jonas yet?*

Marcus had said: *Jonas?*

Anna had said: *Jonas Weber. Have you seen him?*

Marcus had thought about the name.

He had thought about it, in the small careful way of a man doing a small mental search, for a moment. He had not, on the search, come up with anything.

He had said: *I do not think so. Which one is he?*

Anna had, at this, looked at him for a moment.

Anna had said: *Marcus. Jonas Weber. Your Jonas.*

Marcus had said: *I am sorry. I do not — I do not remember a Jonas Weber.*

Anna had, at this, made a small face that Marcus had not, in the moment, been able to interpret. It had been a small face of confusion, and of a small polite social embarrassment, and of a small careful search — Anna, too, doing a small mental check to make sure she was not, herself, misremembering.

She had said, at last: *Marcus. He was your best friend. From — I do not know, from the fifth form onward. You were, throughout everything, always together. He is here. He came in about half an hour ago. He was asking about you.*

Marcus had, at the small bar, felt a small specific cold pass through him.

He had said, quietly: *Anna. I do not remember a Jonas Weber.*

Anna had, at this, looked at him for a longer moment.

She had said, slowly: *you are joking.*

He had said: *I am not.*

She had said: *Marcus. Your Jonas. The one who — the one you spent every summer with. The one who came to your grandmother's funeral. The one who — Marcus, we all knew him. He was in every photograph.*

He had said, more quietly: *I do not — I do not remember any Jonas from that period. I remember Klaus. I remember Stefan. I remember — I remember a great deal. I do not remember a Jonas Weber.*

Anna had, at this, put down her glass.

She had said, in a very small careful voice: *Marcus, come with me.*

She had taken him by the elbow. She had led him across the small room, past several small groups of former classmates, to a small group standing near the window. In the group were Klaus and Stefan and a small woman named Ines whom Marcus had not immediately recognized. In the group, beside Klaus, was a fourth man.

The fourth man had been perhaps Marcus's age. He had been slightly taller than Marcus. He had had dark hair combed back from his forehead. He had been wearing a small navy jacket over a small white shirt. He had had, so far as Marcus could tell from a distance, a small pleasant face.

Anna had said, as they approached: *Jonas. Look who I found.*

The fourth man had turned. He had seen Marcus. His small pleasant face had, at seeing Marcus, opened into the specific small warm smile of a man seeing an old close friend for the first time in twenty years.

He had said, in a small warm voice: *Marcus!*

He had, in the specific small way of an old close friend, opened his arms, and had, before Marcus could quite react, embraced him.

Marcus had, in the small embrace, felt the specific small warmth of a man who was, quite clearly, delighted to see him.

He had, when he had been released, looked at the man.

The man had looked at him. The man's small warm smile had been, on close inspection, entirely genuine.

Marcus had, in the small quiet moment before he was going to have to speak, understood two things.

He had understood, first, that he did not — he had never — known this man.

He had understood, second, that everyone else in the small group was looking at him with the specific small warm expectation of people watching two close friends reunite after twenty years.

He had said, at last, in the specific small careful voice of a man doing a small dishonest thing: *Jonas. It has been — a long time.*

Jonas had said, in his small warm voice: *twenty years. Twenty years, Marcus. My god.*

Klaus had said: *let me get you a drink, Jonas. You are behind.*

Ines had said, to Marcus: *isn't it strange? All this time. It goes so fast.*

Marcus had said, in the small careful voice: *yes.*

He had, at that moment, looked at Anna.

Anna had, on his look, given him the specific small careful look of a woman who had, in the last five minutes, been trying to decide whether her old classmate was making a small strange joke and had, in the small warm reunion of the two friends, come down decisively on the side of yes. She had, in that look, been faintly annoyed with him. She had, in the specific small way of a woman who had briefly been made to feel foolish, given him the small definite look of a woman who was going to give him a small hard time about it later.

Marcus had, at the small group by the window, understood that whatever was happening, no one else in the room was going to help him with it.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man in a small strange situation, decided to spend the rest of the evening finding out what was going on.

—

He had spent the following two hours with Jonas.

He had done this in the specific small careful way of a man conducting a small careful investigation while pretending to conduct a small warm reunion. He had asked, in the small ordinary way of an old friend, what Jonas had been doing over the last twenty years. Jonas had said, in the small warm way of a man happy to be asked, that he had done his engineering degree at the technical university in Karlsruhe, and had, since then, worked as a small structural engineer for a small firm in Munich. He had married a woman named Katrin. They had two children, a boy of nine and a girl of six. He lived in a small suburb of Munich in a small house he had, three years earlier, bought after a long period of saving.

Marcus had asked, in the small casual way of a man asking small casual things, whether he had kept in touch with any of the old group.

Jonas had said: *only through the small annual Christmas card exchange. I saw Klaus once, five years ago, when I was in Hamburg for a conference. Otherwise, no. You know how it is.*

Marcus had said: *and you and I —*

Jonas had said: *the last time was — my god. What was it. My wedding. Ten years ago. You came down for the whole weekend.*

Marcus had, at this, been quiet for a long moment.

He had said: *ten years ago.*

Jonas had said: *yes. You gave the — you gave the speech at the small rehearsal dinner. Do you remember?*

Marcus had said, quietly: *I remember.*

He had not.

He had, throughout the two hours, learned specific small things about Jonas. Jonas had been in his class since the fifth form. Jonas had been, throughout their childhood, his closest friend. Jonas had, at fourteen, been at Marcus's house on the specific weekend Marcus's grandmother had died — Marcus's grandmother, whom he had loved very much, who had died on a Saturday morning in November, and whose funeral Marcus remembered clearly. Jonas had, according to Jonas, been at that funeral. Jonas had, according to Jonas, held Marcus's hand throughout the eulogy.

Marcus had not remembered any of this.

He had, however, remembered the funeral. He had remembered the specific small chapel. He had remembered his mother in a small black dress. He had remembered the specific small feeling of holding — of holding the small worn wooden pew in front of him, because he had not had, that day, anyone specific to hold onto.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man doing a small memory check, tried to remember whether there had been a small quiet friend beside him.

He had not been able to remember one.

But he could not, in the specific small careful way of a man who had been fourteen at the time, be certain there had not been one. His memory of the funeral was, on inspection, not detailed. He remembered the pew. He remembered his mother. He remembered the specific small smell of the chapel. He did not, in any specific way, remember who had been in the pew beside him.

He had, at ten in the evening, said to Jonas: *do you have a photograph? From — from any of it?*

Jonas had said: *of us?*

Marcus had said: *from — from any of the school years. From the summers. From — from something. I would like to see a photograph.*

Jonas had, at this, looked at Marcus for a moment.

Jonas had, then, in the specific small careful way of a man who had understood, quite quickly, that something was slightly wrong, taken out his phone. He had, without ceremony, scrolled through the small archive of his photographs. He had, at last, held up the phone.

The photograph on the screen had been a small photograph of two teenage boys, perhaps sixteen years old, standing together in a small park in what looked like early autumn. They had been wearing the specific small clothing of the mid-two-thousands. They had had their arms around each other's shoulders. They had been laughing.

The boy on the left had been Marcus at sixteen.

The boy on the right had been Jonas.

Marcus had looked at the photograph.

He had looked at it for a long time.

He had, at last, said: *I do not remember this.*

Jonas had, at this, been quiet for a long moment.

Jonas had said, in a small careful voice: *Marcus. Are you all right?*

Marcus had said: *I do not know.*

Jonas had said: *when was the last time you slept.*

Marcus had said: *yesterday. Six hours. It was a normal night.*

Jonas had said, more quietly: *should we — should we get out of here?*

Marcus had said: *yes. I think — I think we should get out of here.*

They had, at ten-fifteen, made their small polite goodbyes to the small group. They had, at ten-twenty, been walking together along the small quiet street outside the restaurant, in the specific soft summer air of a small town in June. Jonas had, on the walk, not said much. He had, in the specific small careful way of a man who had understood something was wrong with his old friend, waited.

Marcus had, at the corner, stopped walking.

He had said, quietly: *Jonas.*

Jonas had said: *yes.*

Marcus had said: *I do not remember you.*

Jonas had said: *I understand.*

Marcus had said: *at all. Not from any period. Not from the funeral. Not from the small trips. Not from — from your wedding. Not from any small summer. I am, at the moment, standing next to a man everyone tells me was my best friend for twelve years, and I do not have any memory of him. I do not have — I do not have a single small image.*

Jonas had said, quietly: *I know.*

Marcus had said: *what do you mean, you know.*

Jonas had, at this, looked at him for a long moment.

Jonas had said, quietly: *because I do not remember you either.*

chapters.title: What the Others Remember
chapters.body:
They had gone to a small quiet bar.

They had sat, over two small glasses of beer, at a small table in the back of the small quiet bar, at ten-forty on a Saturday night in June, and had, in the specific small careful way of two men trying to understand a small strange thing, compared notes.

Jonas had, at the beginning of the conversation, explained.

He had said: *I received the invitation to the reunion two months ago. I did not, when I received it, remember any of the small careful details Anna wrote in the small warm letter she attached. I did not remember you. I did not remember the small close friendship the invitation implied we had had. But when I looked at the class photographs — I have, in my small archive at home, all of the small formal class photographs from the twelve years of gymnasium — I saw myself in them. I saw you in them. I saw us standing together, in the specific small way of close friends, in every one of them from the fifth form onward.*

*I thought, when I saw them, that I must have — must have had a small brain thing. A small quiet stroke. A small area of specific memory loss. I saw my doctor. My doctor examined me. My doctor said I was, on all measures, entirely well. My memory of the last twenty years was perfect. My memory of the twelve years before — of my childhood, of the gymnasium — was, so far as we could tell, largely intact. It was only, in the small strange specific way, one person who was missing.*

*You.*

Marcus had said, quietly: *the same for me.*

Jonas had said: *yes.*

Marcus had said: *when I saw the invitation, I thought — I thought only of the small ordinary classmates I remembered. I thought of Klaus, of Stefan, of Anna. I did not, at any point, think of a Jonas Weber. When Anna said your name tonight, I could not — I could not place it. I had never, in any specific small memory I had, met a Jonas Weber.*

Jonas had said: *and yet.*

Marcus had said: *and yet.*

They had, at the small table, sat with this for a moment.

Marcus had said: *you have photographs.*

Jonas had said: *many.*

Marcus had said: *and the photographs show us — us together. Not — not just in the small class photographs. Not just in the small formal arrangements. But in — in small casual photographs. In the small photographs a close friendship would produce over twelve years.*

Jonas had said: *many. Small photographs at my parents' house. Small photographs at your parents' house. Small photographs on holidays. Small photographs at parties. Small photographs at — at your grandmother's funeral, in the small formal way, in a small envelope your mother sent to my mother afterwards.*

Marcus had said, quietly: *I do not remember your mother.*

Jonas had said: *I do not remember yours.*

They had been quiet.

Marcus had said, at last: *what — what do we do.*

Jonas had said: *I do not know. I have been thinking about it for two months. I have — I have talked to my wife about it. Katrin thinks I should — she thinks I should not worry about it. She thinks it is a small strange thing that happened to me, and that whatever it is, it has been for twenty years, and it has not affected the rest of my life, and I should — I should let it go.*

Marcus had said: *and you?*

Jonas had said: *I came to the reunion. That is my answer.*

Marcus had said: *yes.*

Jonas had said, more quietly: *I wanted to see you. I wanted to see if — if you remembered me. I wanted to know if it was — if it was only me who had lost the memory. I would have found it easier, in some small selfish way, if you had remembered me. I would have — I would have been able to blame my small quiet stroke. I would have been able to accept that I had, in some small way, become the small forgetful one, and that my old close friend had gone on remembering me, and that the whole small strange thing had a small ordinary medical explanation.*

*But you do not remember me.*

Marcus had said: *no.*

Jonas had said: *which means it is not — it is not a small quiet stroke on my part.*

Marcus had said: *no.*

Jonas had said: *which means we have both, in some small strange way, lost the same specific small twelve years of memory.*

Marcus had said: *yes.*

Jonas had said, quietly: *how.*

Marcus had said: *I do not know.*

—

They had sat, at the small back table, until the small quiet bar had closed at one in the morning.

They had, over that time, tried a small number of small careful theories.

The first theory had been that they had, at some specific point in the last twenty years, been involved in a small event that had produced a small mutual traumatic amnesia. This theory had, on inspection, several problems. They had not, so far as either of them could remember, been involved in any such event. And the specific small pattern of the amnesia — the specific loss of only one specific person, and only the memory of that person, and nothing else — did not, so far as either of them knew, correspond to any small medical condition Jonas's doctor had ever heard of.

The second theory had been that they had, at some specific point, gone through some small ordinary falling-out — the kind of small ordinary falling-out that happened to close friends in their early twenties — and had, in the small quiet way of two men not entirely willing to remember an old fight, gradually erased each other from their small useful memories. This theory had, on inspection, also had problems. The erasure was too specific. And the small photographs Jonas had described — the small photographs at Katrin's wedding ten years ago, the small photographs from small trips in the last decade — suggested that the falling-out, if it had happened, had not happened until quite recently.

The third theory had been that one of them was, in the specific small ordinary way, lying.

They had, over the two hours in the small back table, considered this. They had, at last, been unable to make it work. Marcus had, in the small careful way of a man watching another man, been unable to detect any specific small deception in Jonas. Jonas had, in the small careful way of a man watching Marcus, said the same. They had, at the end of the two hours, concluded — in the small honest careful way — that they were probably both telling the truth as they knew it.

The fourth theory had been that they had, in some small strange way, been in two different lives.

Jonas had, at some point during the small consideration of this theory, said: *what if — what if what has happened is that Klaus and Anna and Stefan and Ines have — have all remembered a small history in which you and I were friends, and that we — we have not remembered that history, because it did not happen to us.*

Marcus had said: *and yet the small photographs.*

Jonas had said: *yes.*

Marcus had said: *the small photographs — the small photographs of me at sixteen with a boy I do not know — are, I think, the small definite fact. The photographs happened. Something happened that produced them.*

Jonas had said: *yes.*

Marcus had said: *so we were, at least on the small physical evidence, friends.*

Jonas had said: *at least on the small physical evidence.*

Marcus had said, more quietly: *but we — we do not remember being friends.*

Jonas had said: *no.*

They had sat with this for a long time.

Marcus had said, at last: *what if — what if the small physical evidence is right, and we have both, in some small careful way, been given a small forgetting of it.*

Jonas had said: *who would give us a forgetting.*

Marcus had said: *I do not know. But — but if the alternative is that we are being deceived by everyone we ever knew, and by the small photographs, and by the specific small memory of my grandmother's funeral, and by the small twenty years of your marriage and your children — if the alternative is that all of that is a small conspiracy — then the small forgetting is, at least, the smaller explanation.*

Jonas had said, quietly: *given by whom.*

Marcus had said: *by — by the small careful arrangement of the world.*

Jonas had said: *that is not an answer.*

Marcus had said: *no.*

They had been quiet.

Jonas had said, at last: *and if we — if we, tomorrow, tried to remember.*

Marcus had said: *what do you mean.*

Jonas had said: *I have the small photographs. I have the small letters. I have — I have small objects from that time. If we sat down, tomorrow, in the small hotel room, and we went through them one by one, and we tried to remember — do you think we could?*

Marcus had said, quietly: *I do not know.*

Jonas had said: *I do not either.*

Marcus had said: *do you want to try.*

Jonas had, at this, looked at Marcus for a very long moment.

Jonas had said, at last: *no.*

Marcus had said: *no?*

Jonas had said: *I have thought about this, in the last two months. I have thought — I have thought about what I would do if we found each other tonight, and if we established what we established, and if I had, at last, the small opportunity to sit with an old close friend and to try to remember him.*

*And I have understood, in the last two months, that I do not want to.*

*I have a small careful life, Marcus. I have Katrin. I have my children. I have my small work in Munich. I have — I have, in the specific small careful way of a man of thirty-eight, a life I have made without you. If we sat down tomorrow and tried to remember, and if we — if we found, in some small strange way, that we could — I would have, at the end of the day, a whole new set of memories to carry. I would have, in effect, added twelve years to my life. Twelve years of a friendship I do not currently miss.*

*And I do not — I do not want them, Marcus.*

*I do not want, at thirty-eight, to inherit a childhood I have lived my whole life without.*

Marcus had, at the small back table, looked at him.

Marcus had said, quietly: *I understand.*

Jonas had said: *do you?*

Marcus had said: *yes. Because if you had, tonight, said you did want to — I would have said no.*

Jonas had said: *good.*

They had, at the small back table, sat with the small silent recognition that they had, in the specific small careful way of two men who had, in some way neither of them could name, once been close, agreed on the small important thing.

They had, at one in the morning, walked out of the bar together.

They had, at the corner, said goodnight.

They had, so far as either of them knows, not seen each other again.

chapters.title: The Photograph on the Shelf
chapters.body:
Marcus had, on the following morning, driven back to Hamburg.

He had, on the drive, thought about Jonas.

He had thought about him in the specific small careful way of a man who had, in the last twelve hours, learned that he had had, for twelve years of his childhood, a close friendship he did not remember. He had thought about the small photographs Jonas had shown him. He had thought about the specific small warm face of the young man in the small park in autumn. He had thought about the fact that he had, in his ordinary life at thirty-eight, been walking around for twenty years without ever noticing the absence of that specific small friend.

He had understood, on the drive, that the absence had not, in any specific way, felt like an absence. He had felt, throughout his adult life, entirely complete. He had had, in the specific small way of a man who had not known he was missing anything, the small ordinary satisfactions of an ordinary life. He had loved his wife. He had loved his children. He had, in the small careful way of a small careful man, done his small careful work.

He had not, at any point in the twenty years, been aware of the specific shape of the small absence Jonas had described.

He had understood, on the drive, that this was probably the small careful design of whatever had done it.

Whatever had, in some small strange way, taken the twelve years from him had also taken the shape of them. It had not left, in his memory, a small empty space with an outline. It had, in the specific small careful way, filled the space. His childhood had, in his memory, been full. It had been full in the specific small ways his childhood had, without Jonas, been full — of his family, of his other friends, of the small specific small things he had done alone. He had not, in his memory, been the sort of child who had had a specific small close friend. He had been the sort of child who had done many small things by himself, and who had had a small careful group of ordinary friends, and who had, at eighteen, gone off to university and had not, in any specific way, missed anyone.

That memory had been, so far as he could tell without external evidence, coherent. It had held together. It had, in his ordinary daily life, been the memory he had lived from.

The small photographs Jonas had shown him were the small evidence that the memory was, in some specific small way, not entirely accurate.

Marcus had, on the drive back to Hamburg, understood that he was going to spend the rest of his life carrying this small piece of evidence around, and was going to spend the rest of his life having to decide whether to look at it.

He had, on arrival in Hamburg, decided that he was not going to look at it.

He had decided this in the specific small careful way Jonas had, at the small back table, decided the same thing. He had a small careful life. He had a wife who would, on his telling her the small strange story, not know quite what to do with it. He had children who did not, in the small careful way of children, need any specific small strange story from their father. He had, in the small careful way of a man who had been given a small strange gift, understood that the small strange gift was not, in the specific small way of his current life, a gift he wanted.

He had, on the small Sunday evening in Hamburg after the reunion, told his wife only that the reunion had been small and pleasant and that many of his classmates had grown up in the specific small ordinary ways one grew up.

She had, in the small careful way of a woman who had, over the years, come to understand her husband, not pressed further.

—

He had, over the following years, not thought about Jonas often.

He had, throughout those years, been aware of the small piece of evidence he was carrying. He had, at various small moments in ordinary life, remembered it — when he had, on one occasion, seen a small teenage boy at a small station who had, in some quality of his small stance, reminded him of the boy in Jonas's photograph. When he had, on another occasion, been asked at a small work function whether he had been close to anyone in his childhood. When he had, on a small quiet Sunday, been going through the small box of his own childhood things and had found no small photograph of Jonas in it, and had understood that whatever had taken the memory had also taken the small physical photographs from Marcus's side of the friendship, and had left them, in some specific small careful way, only with Jonas.

He had, at those small moments, thought briefly about Jonas.

He had, at each of those moments, understood that his life had continued, without incident, without the friendship.

He had also, however, understood a small thing that had, over the years, gone on developing in him.

He had understood that if the small careful arrangement of the world had, at some point, taken twelve years of a specific small close friendship from him without his noticing — if the world had had the small careful ability to do that — then the world was, in some quiet way, in the habit of doing this.

He had understood, over the years, that there was, in some small way he could not entirely articulate, an ongoing small careful editing of his life, and that most of it, presumably, he did not know about.

He had understood that Jonas was, in some sense, only the small piece of evidence that had, by the accident of the reunion, come to his attention. That most of the small editing of his life had never come to his attention, because the small evidence for it had also, in the specific small careful way, been taken.

He had, in his middle years, come to think of himself as a man whose life had been, in specific small careful ways, edited.

He had come to think of himself, further, as a man whose life had been edited *for his benefit*.

He had come to this conclusion by a small careful process of elimination. He had considered, in his middle years, whether the editing might have been malicious — whether whatever was doing the small quiet editing was in some sense taking things from him. He had, on considering it, been unable to identify any specific way in which he had, by the editing, been made smaller. His life had been, so far as he could tell, exactly the small careful life he wanted. He had loved his wife. He had loved his children. He had, in the small ordinary way of a small ordinary architect, been satisfied with his work.

If Jonas had been taken from him, Jonas had — so far as he could tell — been taken in the small careful way of a man having a small unnecessary complication removed from a small careful design. His life had been, without Jonas, cleaner. It had been, without Jonas, more coherent. He had, without Jonas, been able to become the specific small careful adult he had become.

He had come to think, over the years, that whatever had been doing the small quiet editing had been doing it kindly.

He had also come to think, over the years, that it had probably done it to many people.

He had come to think, on the whole, that most people in the world had, at various small points in their lives, had specific small pieces of their memory quietly edited, and that most of them, like him, had not noticed.

—

He had, at fifty-nine, retired from the small municipal architecture firm in Hamburg.

He had spent, over the following years, more time at home. His children had, by then, had children of their own. His wife had been the sort of retired woman who, in the small careful way of a Hamburg widow-to-be, had begun to arrange her small life around a small circle of small pleasant friends. Marcus had, in his retirement, done the small ordinary things retired men did — the small careful reading, the small careful cooking, the small careful long walks along the harbor.

He had, at sixty-three, on a small quiet Wednesday afternoon, received a small envelope in the post.

The envelope had been addressed in a small unfamiliar hand. The postmark had been Munich.

Inside the envelope had been a single small photograph.

The photograph had been of an elderly woman in a small hospital bed. She had been perhaps sixty. She had been thin. She had had dark hair that was going white. She had had, on her small tired face, the specific small warm expression of a woman who had, in the last months of her life, become at peace with what was coming.

On the back of the photograph, in a small careful hand, had been written:

*My husband Jonas passed away last month. In his last weeks he asked me to send you this. He said you would understand. — Katrin.*

Marcus had, sitting on the small quiet balcony of his small quiet apartment in Hamburg on a Wednesday afternoon in September, held the small photograph.

He had understood, holding it, several things.

He had understood, first, that Jonas had died.

He had understood, second, that Jonas had, in the last weeks of his life, thought about Marcus. That he had, in the specific small careful way of a man knowing he was leaving, wanted to send some small last acknowledgment to the specific small other man who had, at the reunion twenty-five years earlier, gone through the small strange thing with him.

He had understood, third, that the woman in the photograph was Katrin.
